To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the retinal origin of the visual field asymmetriessuggested in previous studies is supported by the current study, which provides a more complete view on the topic by including anatomical, physiological and psychophysical measures.
retinal structure, retinal function, and visual performance are all asymmetric.

(1) retinal thickness, mfERG, and contrast sensitivity all show a nasal/temporal asymmetry; (2) retinal thickness also shows a superior/inferior pattern of asymmetry; (3) the mfERG P1 shows a nasal/temporal pattern, while the mfERG N95 is more variable; and (4) there are no significant correlations between the different measures of retinal asymmetry.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the retinal anatomy and the visual field.
the investigation of visual asymmetries at different levels (retinal and cortical) and their possible correlation.
the investigation of the relationship between objective retinal asymmetries and visual performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the visual system is indeed asymmetrical, but this asymmetry does not arise in a single location or at a single level of visual processing.
the retinal asymmetries are the most likely source of the observed psychophysical asymmetries.
the retinal asymmetry is the main contributor to psychophysical asymmetry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the retinal mechanisms are asymmetric, with the nasal retina being more efficient than the temporal retina.
the retina is the main contributor for the asymmetries in the visual field.
the retina is not a homogeneous tissue, and its asymmetries have a strong impact on the final visual outcome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
retinal asymmetry is a key determinant of visual performance asymmetry.
the nasal-temporal asymmetries of the retina and visual cortex are likely independent phenomena.
objective measures of retinal function and structure are not necessarily interchangeable, as the same retinal asymmetry may be probed differently depending on the method employed.
